set.layering_notes: Not a multifamily source; recorded so competing uses of Napa County housing money are visible. Terms are from the ADU Forgivable Loan Program Guidelines V2 and loan documents adopted by the Board on March 10, 2026 (Legistar matter 26-308). The County loan is a forgivable construction loan paid into a Managed Construction Escrow Account. Other financing can be layered: the Loan Agreement (Section 3(g)) requires proof that loan proceeds plus other committed funds cover the full construction cost, and up to $2,500 of the rebates pays closing costs on a conventional loan. The County records a Deed of Trust and Regulatory Agreement against the property, and the loan documents allow for senior lienholders, so the County loan can sit behind an existing mortgage. The loan is not transferable: a sale or change in title makes the unforgiven balance due. One loan per primary residence; ADUs already under construction or with a certificate of occupancy are not eligible. The rebate of up to $10,000 for permit and impact fees applies only in the unincorporated County. The V2 guidelines do not name the funding source; the Affordable Housing Fund attribution in typical_award_size comes from 2023 launch materials.
set.audit_note: Prevailing wage re-checked November 10, 2026 against the loan documents attached to the V2 guidelines (matter 26-308): loan agreement, deed of trust, regulatory agreement and note are all with the County of Napa, not the Housing Authority, so the trigger stays false under Labor Code 1720(c)(1). Award terms verified against the same guidelines. Layering notes rewritten November 10, 2026 from the V2 guidelines; the earlier text relied on 2023 search results.

eligible_project_detail: excess surplus plan: affordable homeownership loans and new construction or preservation of affordable rental developments
homelessness prevention and rapid rehousing services (CDC NOFA grants)
set.layering_notes: The Sonoma County Community Development Commission, parent entity of the Sonoma County Housing Authority, is the housing successor. The fund pays for services through the annual CDC NOFA and also finances development directly: $3,837,187 of housing development spending in FY 2024-25 and $1,316,702 in FY 2023-24. The FY 2024-25 report lists Roseland Village (665 Sebastopol Road, Santa Rosa, a former RDA property) and Casa Roseland as under construction but does not tie the development spending to a named project. Its plan for the $1,509,338 excess surplus (held more than 6 years) is reinvestment in affordable homeownership loans and/or new construction or preservation of affordable rental developments, so capital money is possible but is not offered through a posted competitive round. Former RDA Reinvestment and Revitalization money flows into CFH instead. Repayments on the $31,242,980 of loans and grants receivable (the report does not split the two) replenish the fund. The FY 2025-26 report was not posted as of November 10, 2026.
set.audit_note: Corrected November 10, 2026: the FY 2024-25 and FY 2023-24 Housing Successor annual reports show LMIHAF development spending ($3,837,187 and $1,316,702), so the record no longer says the fund is not used for development. FY 2025-26 report not yet posted. Prevailing wage left unclear: no LMIHAF document states a rule, 1720(c)(1) likely unavailable because the housing successor is the CDC (parent of the Housing Authority), and 1720(c)(5)(E) turns on project facts. funding_type changed from grant to loan November 10, 2026: FY 2024-25 housing development spending ($3,837,187) was about 22 times homelessness services spending ($173,658), Note 4 of the report describes the $31,242,980 receivable as loans receivable, and the excess surplus plan names homeownership loans and rental development. The report does not state the instrument for each development expenditure, so loan is an inference from these facts. The only posted round is the CDC NOFA for services grants (see cycle_notes).
